claim: Herpes simplex virus-1 (HSV-1) replicates within the nucleus coopting the host's RNA Polymerase II (Pol II) machinery for production of viral mRNAs culminating in host transcriptional shut off.
source: Herpes simplex virus-1 (HSV-1) replicates within the nucleus coopting the host's RNA Polymerase II (Pol II) machinery for production of viral mRNAs culminating in host transcriptional shut off.
evidence: This is a general statement about HSV-1 biology that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: ICP4 is responsible for preferential recruitment of the Pol II machinery to the viral genome.
source: We identified ICP4 as responsible for preferential recruitment of the Pol II machinery to the viral genome.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly ChIP-Seq experiments comparing WT and ICP4-null infections.

claim: ICP4 is a viral nucleoprotein which binds double-stranded DNA.
source: ICP4 is a viral nucleoprotein which binds double-stranded DNA.
evidence: This is supported by both established knowledge and data presented in the manuscript showing ICP4 binding patterns.

claim: ICP4 discriminately binds the viral genome due to the absence of cellular nucleosomes and high density of cognate binding sites.
source: We determined ICP4 discriminately binds the viral genome due to the absence of cellular nucleosomes and high density of cognate binding sites.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq data showing ICP4 binding patterns, ATAC-Seq data showing genome accessibility, and histone ChIP-Seq data.

claim: ICP4's ability to recruit TBP and Mediator creates a competitive transcriptional environment.
source: We posit that ICP4's ability to recruit not just Pol II, but also more limiting essential components, such as TBP and Mediator, create a competitive transcriptional environment.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq data showing recruitment of these factors and is presented as an interpretation of the data.

claim: The genome of Herpes simplex virus-1 (HSV-1) is transcribed by RNA Polymerase II (Pol II).
source: Like most DNA viruses, the genome of Herpes simplex virus-1 (HSV-1) is transcribed by RNA Polymerase II (Pol II) (Alwine et al., 1974).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: HSV-1 has approximately 85 genes.
source: Its approximately 85 genes (McGeoch et al., 1988; McGeoch et al., 1986; McGeoch et al., 1985)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior genomic characterization studies.

claim: HSV-1 genes are transcribed in a temporally coordinated sequence.
source: are transcribed in a temporally coordinated sequence, such that their protein products are expressed at the appropriate time in the life cycle of the virus (Honess and Roizman, 1974a; Honess and Roizman, 1974b; Honess and Roizman, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on HSV-1 gene expression kinetics.

claim: Immediate early (IE) gene products enable the efficient expression of early (E) and late (L) genes.
source: Immediate early (IE) gene products enable the efficient expression of early (E) and late (L) genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HSV-1 gene expression cascade.

claim: Early gene protein products are mostly involved in DNA replication.
source: The protein products of E genes are mostly involved in DNA replication.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HSV-1 early gene functions.

claim: DNA replication and IE proteins enable the efficient transcription of L genes, which encode the structural components of the virus.
source: DNA replication and IE proteins enable the efficient transcription of L genes, which encode the structural components of the virus.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HSV-1 late gene expression and function.

claim: DNA replication licenses L promoters, enabling the binding of core Pol II transcription factors, thus activating the initiation of L transcription.
source: DNA replication licenses L promoters, enabling the binding of core Pol II transcription factors, thus activating the initiation of L transcription (Dremel and DeLuca, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The entire transcriptional cascade is observed within 3 hour post entry.
source: This entire transcriptional cascade is observed within 3 hour (h) post entry (Dembowski and DeLuca, 2018; Dremel and DeLuca, 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Production of the first viral progeny occurs between 4 and 6 h post-infection (hpi).
source: culminating in production of the first viral progeny between 4 and 6 h post-infection (hpi).
evidence: This is established knowledge about HSV-1 replication kinetics.

claim: ICP4 is essential for viral growth because it promotes efficient transcription of viral E and L genes.
source: ICP4 is essential for viral growth because it promotes efficient transcription of viral E and L genes (Dixon and Schaffer, 1980; Preston, 1979; Watson and Clements, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior genetic studies.

claim: In the absence of ICP4, E and L proteins are poorly expressed, IE proteins are overproduced, DNA replication does not occur, and there is no detectable viral yield.
source: Thus, in the absence of ICP4, E and L proteins are poorly expressed, IE proteins are overproduced, DNA replication does not occur, and there is no detectable viral yield (DeLuca et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work characterizing ICP4-null mutants.

claim: ICP4 was first shown to bind to DNA cellulose made from salmon sperm DNA.
source: ICP4 was first shown to bind to DNA cellulose made from salmon sperm DNA (Powell and Purifoy, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: ICP4 has sequence-specific DNA binding activity.
source: Faber and Wilcox (1986) later showed ICP4 has sequence-specific DNA binding activity.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: ICP4 interacts with a number of cellular general transcription factors (GTFs), predominantly components of TFIID and the Mediator complex.
source: ICP4 interacts with a number of cellular general transcription factors (GTFs), predominantly components of TFIID and the Mediator complex (Carrozza and DeLuca, 1996; Lester and DeLuca, 2011; Wagner and DeLuca, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ICP4 facilitates recruitment of GTFs to the viral genome through its DNA binding activity.
source: facilitating their recruitment to the viral genome through its DNA binding activity (Dembowski and DeLuca, 2018; Lester and DeLuca, 2011; Sampath and Deluca, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ICP4 is synthesized early in infection, binds to the viral genome located at ND10 structures, and remains associated with the genome throughout all phases of infection.
source: ICP4 is synthesized early in infection, binds to the viral genome located at ND10 structures (Everett et al., 2003), and remains associated with the genome throughout all phases of infection (Dembowski and DeLuca, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Epigenetic modulation of histones associated with the viral genome early in infection can affect productive viral infection.
source: Studies have also shown that epigenetic modulation of histones associated with the viral genome early in infection can affect productive viral infection (Knipe and Cliffe, 2008; Liang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The abundance of histones is relatively low or absent on viral genomes during productive infection.
source: However, we have shown that the abundance of histones is relatively low or absent, and that ICP4 is one of the most abundant proteins on viral genomes during productive infection (Dembowski and DeLuca, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: ICP4 is one of the most abundant proteins on viral genomes during productive infection.
source: However, we have shown that the abundance of histones is relatively low or absent, and that ICP4 is one of the most abundant proteins on viral genomes during productive infection (Dembowski and DeLuca, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: ICP4 is a major component of viral nucleoprotein, which functions in place of traditional cellular chromatin.
source: We propose that ICP4 is a major component of viral nucleoprotein, which functions in place of traditional cellular chromatin, and allows for the robust recruitment of cellular transcription factors specifically to the viral genome.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: ICP4 densely coated the viral genome early during infection (two hpi).
source: Early during infection (two hpi) ICP4 densely coated the viral genome (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Viral genome replication decreased the amount of ICP4 bound per genome.
source: Viral genome replication decreased the amount of ICP4 bound per genome (Figure 1A–B)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 1.

claim: By six hpi ICP4 binding was retained exclusively on strong ICP4 binding motifs.
source: By six hpi ICP4 binding was retained exclusively on strong ICP4 binding motifs (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Some of the retained ICP4 binding sites were those previously established as having an inhibitory effect on the gene promoter bound, including ORF P, ICP4, and LAT.
source: Some of the retained binding sites were those previously established as having an inhibitory effect on the gene promoter bound, including ORF P, ICP4, and LAT (Figure 1D).
evidence: This combines data from Figure 1 with established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: The location and number of high confidence ICP4 occupied sites did not alter significantly throughout infection.
source: A closer analysis of ICP4 peaks demonstrated that the location and number of high confidence occupied sites did not alter significantly throughout infection (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by peak calling analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The amount of ICP4 bound between distinct peaks decreased as genome number increased.
source: Instead the amount of ICP4 bound between distinct peaks decreased as genome number increased (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The ICP4 consensus binding motif is DTSGKBDTBNHSG, where D is A, G, T; S is C or G; K is G or T; B is C, G, T; H is A, C, T.
source: DTSGKBDTBNHSG was the only motif discovered (Figure 1F), where D is A, G, T; S is C or G; K is G or T; B is C, G, T; H is A, C, T.
evidence: This is supported by motif discovery analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The ICP4 binding motif discovered is similar to that previously discovered using in vitro techniques, RTCGTCNNYNYSG.
source: This binding motif is similar to that previously discovered using in vitro techniques, RTCGTCNNYNYSG (DiDonato et al., 1991).
evidence: This compares the current data to prior work cited.

claim: ICP4 binds to specific sites, but also coats the genome early in infection forming a type of nucleoprotein.
source: These results demonstrate that ICP4 binds to specific sites, but also coats the genome early in infection forming a type of nucleoprotein.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ChIP-Seq data presented.

claim: Due to mass action, ICP4-nucleoprotein changes as infection proceeds, limiting binding to predominantly strong cognate binding sites as the number of genomes increase due to replication.
source: Due to mass action, ICP4-nucleoprotein changes as infection proceeds, limiting binding to predominantly strong cognate binding sites as the number of genomes increase due to replication.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on mass action principles.

claim: In n12 infection, there was a decrease in binding for all the factors to most viral promoters, with the exception of IE genes where there was an increase in binding.
source: In n12 infection, we observed a decrease in binding for all the factors to most viral promoters, with the exception of IE genes (Figure 2A–B), where there was an increase in binding.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq data comparing n12 and WT infections shown in Figure 2.

claim: There were detectable, although highly reduced, peaks of TBP and SP1 binding to the UL23 promoter in the absence of ICP4.
source: There were detectable, although highly reduced, peaks of TBP and SP1 binding to the UL23 promoter in the absence of ICP4.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq data.

claim: TBP and SP1 binding sites at UL23 are functional in the n12 background reflecting the basal binding activity of TBP and SP1.
source: It has been previously shown that these sites are functional in the n12 background reflecting the basal binding activity of TBP and SP1 (Imbalzano et al., 1991) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This combines current data with a citation to prior work.

claim: TBP and SP1 bound to selective E promoters in the absence of ICP4, namely UL23, UL29, UL39, and UL50.
source: Similar to UL23 we observed TBP and SP1 bound to selective E promoters in the absence of ICP4, namely UL23, UL29, UL39, and UL50 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ICP4 is packaged into the tegument of virions.
source: ICP4 is packaged into the tegument of virions (Yao and Courtney, 1989)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Wild type ICP4 is packaged into n12 virions.
source: which results in packaging of wild type ICP4 into n12 virions (Dembowski and DeLuca, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The amount of ICP4 binding from the virion to DNA is not sufficient to promote transcription complexes on viral early and late genes.
source: While the ultimate source of these reads is not clear at present, the amount of binding of ICP4 from the virion to DNA is not sufficient to promote transcription complexes on viral early and late genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-Seq data showing minimal ICP4 binding in n12 infection and lack of E/L gene expression.

claim: Med1 and Med23 bound the viral genome with an almost identical pattern, indicating they are parts of the Mediator complex bound early during viral infection.
source: Med1 and Med23 bound the viral genome with an almost identical pattern (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2), indicating they are parts of the Mediator complex bound early during viral infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar binding patterns observed in ChIP-Seq data.

claim: In WT infected cells, the binding of Mediator concentrated near the starts sites of ICP4-induced viral genes.
source: In WT infected cells, the binding of Mediator concentrated near the starts sites of ICP4-induced viral genes.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq data for Med1 and Med23.

claim: The Mediator complex densely coated the viral genome, resembling the ICP4 binding pattern.
source: However, the Mediator complex also densely coated the viral genome, resembling the ICP4 binding pattern.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq data comparing ICP4 and Mediator binding patterns.

claim: The dense coating of Mediator on the viral genome was completely absent in n12 infection.
source: This dense coating was completely absent in n12 infection, demonstrating this phenotype is not an artifact of the IP.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq data comparing WT and n12 infections.

claim: ICP4 and Mediator interact.
source: We suspect this reflects the fact that ICP4 and Mediator interact.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar binding patterns and is supported by prior citations showing protein-protein interactions.

claim: In the absence of ICP4, the binding of Pol II was reduced the most compared to the other transcription factors.
source: In the absence of ICP4, the binding of Pol II was reduced the most compared to the other transcription factors (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The magnified difference in Pol II binding is likely a result of the cooperative nature of Pol II recruitment requiring multiple protein-protein interactions.
source: This magnified difference is likely a result of the cooperative nature of Pol II recruitment requiring multiple protein-protein interactions.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on established knowledge of transcription factor cooperativity.

claim: ICP4 was required for robust recruitment of all GTF's tested, cooperatively recruiting Pol II to E and L promoters.
source: In summary ICP4 was required for robust recruitment of all GTF's tested, cooperatively recruiting Pol II to E and L promoters (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 2.

claim: IE promoters retained robust GTF recruitment via an independent mechanism involving a complex consisting of Oct-1, HCF and VP16 binding to TAATGARAT promoter elements.
source: IE promoters retained robust GTF recruitment via an independent mechanism involving a complex consisting of Oct-1, HCF and VP16 binding to TAATGARAT promoter elements (Preston et al., 1988; Stern and Herr, 1991; Stern et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on IE promoter regulation.

claim: In both WT and n12 infection, the number of H3 reads mapped to the viral genome was 100-fold less than ICP4.
source: We found in both WT and n12 infection that the number of H3 reads mapped to the viral genome was 100-fold less than ICP4
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of ChIP-Seq data.

claim: The H3 binding pattern on the viral genome was nearly identical to input reads, with R2 correlations of 0.0004 and 0.02.
source: and the pattern was nearly identical to input reads (Figure 3A), with R2 correlations of 0.0004 and 0.02 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: H3 binding to the viral genome was minimal and not reproducible.
source: These data demonstrated H3 binding to the viral genome was minimal and not reproducible.
evidence: This is concluded from the ChIP-Seq data analysis.

claim: H3 binding was still minimal in the absence of ICP4 (n12).
source: Furthermore, H3 binding was still minimal in the absence of ICP4 (n12).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq data from n12 infection.

claim: The number and quality of H3 reads mapped to the cellular genome was approximately 10 million with R2 correlations of ≥0.97.
source: This was not due to technical issues as the number and quality of H3 reads mapped to the cellular genome for the same samples was approximately 10 million with R2 correlations of ≥0.97 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by quality control analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: A similar trend was seen with H3K4me3, H3K27ac, H3K9me3, and H3K27me3 reads mapped to the viral genome.
source: We saw a similar trend with H3K4me3, H3K27ac, H3K9me3, and H3K27me3 reads mapped to the viral genome (Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: Even tagmentation was observed in both WT and n12 conditions on the viral genome.
source: We observed even tagmentation in both conditions (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-Seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The viral genome lacked nucleosomal laddering visible on the cellular genome.
source: absent the nucleosomal laddering visible on the cellular genome (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-Seq fragment size analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The viral genome in n12 and WT was 2.2 and 2-fold more accessible than the cellular genome.
source: Quantification of ATAC-Seq reads determined that the viral genome in n12 and WT was 2.2 and 2-fold more accessible than the cellular genome (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of ATAC-Seq data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The viral genome was much more accessible than the cellular genome, and this increased accessibility was not ICP4-dependent.
source: We conclude that the viral genome was much more accessible than the cellular genome, and this increased accessibility was not ICP4-dependent.
evidence: This is concluded from ATAC-Seq data comparing WT and n12 infections.

claim: ICP4 binding and GTF recruitment, not viral genome accessibility, was responsible for robust GTF binding.
source: ICP4 binding and GTF recruitment, not viral genome accessibility, was responsible for robust GTF binding.
evidence: This is concluded from the combination of ChIP-Seq and ATAC-Seq data.

claim: ICP4 bound to the cellular genome in a manner quite distinctive from the pattern observed on the viral genome.
source: ICP4 bound to the cellular genome in a manner quite distinctive from the pattern observed on the viral genome.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq data aligned to the cellular genome.

claim: ICP4 only bound in distinct peaks around cellular transcription start sites (TSS) of a subset of cellular genes.
source: ICP4 only bound in distinct peaks around cellular transcription start sites (TSS) of a subset of cellular genes (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Genes bound by ICP4 grouped ontologically to common housekeeping functions including pathways related to chromatin, transcription, and metabolism.
source: These genes grouped ontologically to common housekeeping functions including pathways related to chromatin, transcription, and metabolism (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by ontology analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: ICP4 binding to the cellular genome reduced from 2 to 4 hpi, and became negligible at six hpi.
source: This binding reduced from 2 to 4 hpi, and became negligible at six hpi (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is supported by time course ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 4.

claim: At two hpi ICP4 bound to the cellular genome at 5727 sites or 0.002 peaks per kbp.
source: At two hpi ICP4 bound to the cellular genome at 5727 sites (Figure 4E) or 0.002 peaks per kbp
evidence: This is supported by peak calling analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: ICP4 bound to the viral genome at 122 sites or 0.8 peaks per kbp.
source: whereas ICP4 bound to the viral genome at 122 sites (Figure 1E) or 0.8 peaks per kbp.
evidence: This is supported by peak calling analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: There was a much greater density of ICP4 binding motifs present in the viral genome (two motifs/kbp) than the cellular genome (0.02 motifs/kbp).
source: Similar we found a much greater density of ICP4 binding motifs present in the viral genome (two motifs/kbp) than the cellular genome (0.02 motifs/kbp).
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis of viral and cellular genomes.

claim: ICP4 binding peaks that did not localize at an ICP4 binding consensus were observed, suggesting that ICP4 may associate with the cellular genome by an alternative mechanism.
source: We observed ICP4 binding peaks that did not localize at an ICP4 binding consensus (Figure 4A) suggesting that ICP4 may associate with the cellular genome by an alternative mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ICP4 bound to the cellular genome early during infection, when the relative concentration of ICP4 to viral genomes is still quite high.
source: We conclude that ICP4 bound to the cellular genome early during infection, when the relative concentration of ICP4 to viral genomes is still quite high.
evidence: This is concluded from the time course ChIP-Seq data.

claim: The amount of ICP4 on the cellular genome quickly dropped off as viral genome number increased and ICP4 preferentially bound to the viral genome.
source: The amount of ICP4 on the cellular genome quickly dropped off as viral genome number increased and ICP4 preferentially bound to the viral genome.
evidence: This is concluded from the time course ChIP-Seq data.

claim: ICP4 specifically bound where there was an absence of histones, adjacent to euchromatic markers.
source: Furthermore, we found that ICP4 specifically bound where there was an absence of histones, adjacent to euchromatic markers.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq data comparing ICP4 binding with histone modifications.

claim: ICP4 did not alter the chromatic markers of the promoters it bound to.
source: ICP4 did not alter the chromatic markers of the promoters it bound to
evidence: This is concluded from comparing infected and uninfected ChIP-Seq data for histone modifications.

claim: ICP4 bound regions which were also accessible in the absence of infection.
source: rather ICP4 bound regions which were also accessible in the absence of infection.
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-Seq data comparing infected and uninfected cells.

claim: ICP4's ability to bind naked double-stranded DNA in a sequence independent manner is promoted by ICP4 multimerization.
source: This likely reflects ICP4's ability to bind naked double-stranded DNA in a sequence independent manner. This ability is promoted by ICP4 multimerization (Kuddus and DeLuca, 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on ICP4 multimerization.

claim: The GTF's present on cellular promoters, namely TFIID and Mediator complex, may further stabilize ICP4 binding at these promoters via their well-characterized interactions.
source: The GTF's present on these cellular promoters, namely TFIID and Mediator complex, may further stabilize ICP4 binding at these promoters via their well-characterized interactions (Carrozza and DeLuca, 1996; Lester and DeLuca, 2011; Wagner and DeLuca, 2013).
evidence: This is speculated based on known protein-protein interactions cited.

claim: TSS with high ICP4 binding were also bound by Pol II and adjacent to euchromatic markers.
source: TSS with high ICP4 binding were also bound by Pol II and adjacent to euchromatic markers.
evidence: This is supported by k-means clustering analysis of ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: TSS with low ICP4 binding were associated with only heterochromatic markers.
source: TSS with low ICP4 binding were associated with only heterochromatic markers.
evidence: This is supported by k-means clustering analysis of ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Genes clustered as high ICP4 binding had higher tagmentation frequency when assessed using ATAC-Seq.
source: Furthermore, genes clustered as high ICP4 binding had higher tagmentation frequency when assessed using ATAC-Seq (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-Seq data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The binding pattern of ICP4 was directly related (Spearman coefficient ≥0.5) to Pol II and cellular euchromatin, clustering as most similar to H3K27ac and H3K4me3.
source: We found that the binding pattern of ICP4 was directly related (Spearman coefficient ≥0.5) to Pol II and cellular euchromatin, clustering as most similar to H3K27ac and H3K4me3 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by Spearman correlation analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The heterochromatic markers, H3K9me3 and H3K27me3, clustered together, and were not correlated (Spearman coefficient ~0) to ICP4 or cellular chromatin.
source: The heterochromatic markers, H3K9me3 and H3K27me3, clustered together, and were not correlated (Spearman coefficient ~0) to ICP4 or cellular chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by Spearman correlation analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: ICP4 bound regions had little overlap with their cognate binding motifs.
source: Interestingly, ICP4 bound regions had little overlap with their cognate binding motifs (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by peak intersection analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: 82% of ICP4 bound regions were within 1 kb of a promoter.
source: A closer analysis of the actual genomic region where each factor bound, revealed that 82% of ICP4 bound regions were within 1 kb of a promoter (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by ChIPSeeker analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Only 10% of ICP4 predicted binding motifs were within 1 kb of a promoter.
source: By comparison only 10% of ICP4 predicted binding motifs were within 1 kb of a promoter.
evidence: This is supported by motif location analysis.

claim: The euchromatic regions of the cellular genome that were occupied by ICP4 in infected cells were also euchromatic in uninfected cells.
source: Furthermore, the euchromatic regions of the cellular genome that were occupied by ICP4 in infected cells were also euchromatic in uninfected cells, indicating that ICP4 does not globally promote open chromatin in these regions of the genome (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is supported by comparing ChIP-Seq and ATAC-Seq data from infected and uninfected cells.

claim: ICP4 does not globally promote open chromatin in regions of the cellular genome where it binds.
source: indicating that ICP4 does not globally promote open chromatin in these regions of the genome (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is concluded from comparing chromatin accessibility in infected and uninfected cells.

claim: ICP4 is able to bind nonspecifically to accessible regions of the cellular genome, namely active promoters, early in infection when the relative concentration of ICP4 is high.
source: These data support a model in which ICP4 is able to bind nonspecifically to accessible regions of the cellular genome, namely active promoters, early in infection when the relative concentration of ICP4 is high.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the data presented.

claim: Depletion in Pol II binding to cellular promoters occurs with HSV-1 infection.
source: We observed depletion in Pol II binding to cellular promoters with infection (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Prior studies assessed HSV-1 infection post-replication at three, four, or six hpi and observed Pol II depletion.
source: This observation is consistent with prior studies, which assessed HSV-1 infection post-replication at three, four, or six hpi (Abrisch et al., 2015; Birkenheuer et al., 2018; McSwiggen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Depletion of Pol II occupancy on cellular mRNA promoters only occurred in WT infection, not in n12 infection.
source: We observed depletion of Pol II occupancy on cellular mRNA promoters only in WT infection (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq data comparing WT and n12 infections shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: ICP4 was required for depletion of Pol II from host mRNA promoters, and this effect was independent of viral genome copy number.
source: Thus we concluded that ICP4 was required for depletion of Pol II from host mRNA promoters, and this effect was independent of viral genome copy number.
evidence: This is concluded from ChIP-Seq data comparing WT and n12 infections at 2 hpi (pre-replication).

claim: Significant depletion of Pol II from cellular promoters was observed in permissive and shifted tsKos samples.
source: We observed significant depletion of Pol II from cellular promoters in permissive and shifted samples (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq data from tsKos temperature shift experiments shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: Pol II depletion was not directly related to viral genome copy number.
source: Pol II depletion was not directly related to viral genome copy number.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing tsKos conditions with different genome copy numbers.

claim: tsKos shifted up had the highest number of viral genomes present, but did not reach the same level of cellular Pol II depletion as cells grown at permissive temperature for the same length of time.
source: tsKos shifted up had the highest number of viral genomes present, but did not reach the same level of cellular Pol II depletion as cells grown at permissive temperature for the same length of time.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq data from tsKos experiments.

claim: The viral genome is not solely responsible for preferential recruitment of cellular Pol II.
source: These data suggest that the viral genome is not solely responsible for preferential recruitment of cellular Pol II.
evidence: This is concluded from the tsKos temperature shift experiments.

claim: ICP4 bound to the viral genome is required for depletion of Pol II from cellular promoters.
source: Instead ICP4 bound to the viral genome is required for depletion of Pol II from cellular promoters.
evidence: This is concluded from the combination of n12 and tsKos experiments.

claim: As the number of ICP4 bound viral genomes increased, there was a corresponding decrease in Pol II on host promoters.
source: As the number of ICP4 bound viral genomes increased, we observed a corresponding decrease in Pol II on host promoters.
evidence: This is concluded from the tsKos time course experiments.

claim: ICP4 bound promiscuously to the viral genome prior to DNA replication.
source: Our data demonstrated that ICP4 bound promiscuously to the viral genome prior to DNA replication.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq data at 2 hpi.

claim: At early time points, the relative concentration of ICP4 to viral genomes was relatively high which likely promoted multimerization on DNA through ICP4-ICP4 interactions.
source: At this time point, the relative concentration of ICP4 to viral genomes was relatively high which likely promoted multimerization on DNA through ICP4-ICP4 interactions (Kuddus and DeLuca, 2007).
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by a citation on ICP4 multimerization.

claim: Components of Mediator bound generally to the viral genome, concentrating near viral TATA boxes.
source: Components of Mediator bound generally to the viral genome, concentrating near viral TATA boxes.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq data for Med1 and Med23.

claim: Mediator binding to the viral genome is a unique recruitment phenotype which binds exclusively at cellular TSS via multiple protein-protein interactions.
source: This is a unique recruitment phenotype for Mediator which binds exclusively at cellular TSS via multiple protein-protein interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing Mediator binding patterns on viral vs cellular genomes.

claim: In the absence of ICP4, Mediator interactions were not sufficient to support Mediator binding to the viral genome, with the exception of IE promoters.
source: In the absence of ICP4, these interactions were not sufficient to support Mediator binding to the viral genome. With the exception of Mediator recruitment to IE promoters which does not require ICP4 and reflects the activity of VP16 (Batterson and Roizman, 1983; Campbell et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq data from n12 infection and citations on VP16 function.

claim: There was a 2 to 10-fold decrease in recruitment of Pol II, TBP, and Sp1 to viral E and L promoters without ICP4.
source: Similarly, we observed a 2 to 10-fold decrease in recruitment of Pol II, TBP, and Sp1 to viral E and L promoters without ICP4.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of ChIP-Seq data comparing WT and n12.

claim: The minimal level of GTF recruitment in the absence of ICP4 is insufficient to support transcription, which explains why only IE transcripts are efficiently transcribed in the absence of ICP4.
source: This minimal level of recruitment is insufficient to support transcription, which explains why only IE transcripts are efficiently transcribed in the absence of ICP4.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-Seq data and established knowledge of n12 phenotype.

claim: ICP4-dependent GTF recruitment was not due to a global accessibility change.
source: ICP4-dependent GTF recruitment was not due to a global accessibility change.
evidence: This is concluded from ATAC-Seq data comparing WT and n12 infections.

claim: In the absence of ICP4 the viral genome remained absent of histones and had little change in tagmentation frequency.
source: In the absence of ICP4 the viral genome remained absent of histones and had little change in tagmentation frequency.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq and ATAC-Seq data from n12 infection.

claim: The absence of histones on the viral genome in n12 infection is most likely due to the action of ICP0, which is an IE protein expressed in the absence of ICP4 and has been shown to preclude histones from the genome.
source: This is most likely due to the action of ICP0, which is an IE protein expressed in the absence of ICP4 and has been shown to preclude histones from the genome (Cliffe and Knipe, 2008; Ferenczy and DeLuca, 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citations on ICP0 function.

claim: ICP4's ability to interact and recruit Mediator and TFIID generally to the viral genome creates a local concentration gradient.
source: We posit that ICP4's ability to interact and recruit Mediator and TFIID generally to the viral genome creates a local concentration gradient.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data.

claim: The local concentration gradient created by ICP4 increases the incidence of Pol II transcription machinery recruitment to the viral genome, which is stabilized by contact with additional protein-DNA, protein-protein interactions.
source: Ultimately this increases the incidence of Pol II transcription machinery recruitment to the viral genome, which is stabilized by contact with additional protein-DNA, protein-protein interactions.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the data.

claim: ICP4 coating the viral genome is a unique recruitment phenotype for a protein that functions in GTF recruitment and likely reflects the architecture of the viral genome.
source: Our observation that ICP4 coats the viral genome, a unique recruitment phenotype for a protein that functions in GTF recruitment likely reflects the architecture of the viral genome.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data.

claim: The condensed organization of the HSV genome results in overlap of viral promoters and ORFS, with little to no unused coding space.
source: The condensed organization of the HSV genome results in overlap of viral promoters and ORFS, with little to no unused coding space.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HSV genome organization.

claim: It may be advantageous for ICP4 to generally and dynamically bind to the viral genome due to the condensed organization of the HSV genome.
source: For these reasons, it may be advantageous for ICP4 to generally and dynamically bind to the viral genome.
evidence: This is speculation based on the genome organization and ICP4 binding data.

claim: The relatively high density of ICP4 on the viral genome prior to DNA replication may serve to repress transcription of the true late promoters, which only contain binding sites for the core GTFs.
source: It is also possible that the relatively high density of ICP4 on the viral genome prior to DNA replication may serve to repress transcription of the true late promoters, which only contain binding sites for the core GTFs.
evidence: This is speculation based on the ICP4 binding pattern and known late promoter characteristics.

claim: ICP4 binding can impose an increased dependence on DNA replication for expression from relatively simple promoters.
source: It has been shown that ICP4 binding can impose an increased dependence on DNA replication for expression from relatively simple promoters (Koop et al., 1993; Rivera-Gonzalez et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ICP4 serves a critical role as a general viral transcription factor, essential for activation and continued transcription of E and L genes.
source: These data demonstrated the critical role ICP4 serves as a general viral transcription factor, essential for activation and continued transcription of E and L genes.
evidence: This is concluded from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: ICP4 possesses the ability to bind to double stranded DNA independent of sequence, an ability that is facilitated by ICP4 oligomerization on the genome.
source: ICP4 possesses the ability to bind to double stranded DNA independent of sequence, an ability that is facilitated by ICP4 oligomerization on the genome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ICP4 biochemical properties.

claim: The high density of ICP4 binding motifs on the viral genome aggregate to create a global affinity for ICP4.
source: Instead the high density of ICP4 binding motifs on the viral genome aggregate to create a global affinity for ICP4.
evidence: This is inferred from the motif density analysis and binding data.

claim: The high density of ICP4 binding motifs provides an explanation for why no specific binding sites on the genome affect the ability of ICP4 to activate transcription.
source: This coating phenotype provides an explanation for why no specific binding sites on the genome affect the ability of ICP4 to activate transcription (Coen et al., 1986; Smiley et al., 1992).
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citations to prior genetic studies.

claim: The binding preference of ICP4 for the viral genome is due to the 100-fold higher density of cognate binding sites and absence of cellular histones.
source: We propose that the binding preference of ICP4 for the viral genome is due to the 100-fold higher density of cognate binding sites and absence of cellular histones.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the motif density and histone ChIP-Seq data.

claim: HSV-1 productive infection generates 1,000–10,000 viral progeny per infected cell within a 24 h window.
source: HSV-1 productive infection generates 1,000–10,000 viral progeny per infected cell within a 24 h window.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HSV-1 replication.

claim: By six hpi viral mRNA's comprise almost 50% of the total mRNA present in the host nucleus.
source: By six hpi viral mRNA's comprise almost 50% of the total mRNA present in the host nucleus (Dremel and DeLuca, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Binding of Pol II to cellular promoters dramatically decreases upon HSV-1 infection.
source: Furthermore, binding of Pol II to cellular promoters dramatically decreases upon HSV-1 infection (Abrisch et al., 2015; Birkenheuer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A recent study concluded that viral replication compartments efficiently enrich Pol II into membraneless domains.
source: A recent study concluded that viral replication compartments efficiently enrich Pol II into membraneless domains (McSwiggen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: McSwiggen et al. proposed that Pol II enrichment was dependent on the absence of nucleosomes which made the viral genome 100-fold more accessible than the cellular genome.
source: McSwiggen et al. proposed this phenomenon was dependent on the absence of nucleosomes which made the viral genome 100-fold more accessible than the cellular genome.
evidence: This is a summary of a prior study's conclusions.

claim: Viral genome accessibility is critical for viral infection and is essential for ICP4 binding.
source: While we agree that this accessibility is critical for viral infection, we believe it is essential for ICP4 binding.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their data in the context of prior work.

claim: Similar to cellular chromatin, ICP4 coats the viral genome throughout productive infection.
source: Similar to cellular chromatin, ICP4 coats the viral genome throughout productive infection (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by the ChIP-Seq data and summarized in Figure 7.

claim: ICP4 functions to scaffold Pol II transcription machinery to the viral genome.
source: However, ICP4 also functions to scaffold Pol II transcription machinery to the viral genome.
evidence: This is concluded from the ChIP-Seq data showing GTF recruitment.

claim: One or more components of the PIC, such as the ICP4 binding partners TFIID and Mediator, are limiting.
source: We propose that one or more components of the PIC, such as the ICP4 binding partners TFIID and Mediator, are limiting and ICP4 recruits these factors to the viral genome.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data.

claim: As the number of viral genomes bound by ICP4 increases, the limiting PIC components no longer contacts cellular promoters.
source: As the number of viral genomes bound by ICP4 increases, the limiting PIC components no longer contacts cellular promoters.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the data.

claim: Decreased Pol II occupancy on host promoters prevents cellular transcription.
source: Ultimately this results in decreased Pol II occupancy on host promoters, preventing cellular transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the Pol II ChIP-Seq data on cellular promoters.

claim: The mechanism of ICP4-mediated GTF sequestration is essential to facilitate the rapidly progressing infection while limiting the extent to which the host can respond to viral challenge.
source: This mechanism is essential to facilitate the rapidly progressing infection while limiting the extent to which the host can respond to viral challenge.
evidence: This is speculation about the biological significance of the findings.

claim: The approximate number of genomes per cell in WT and n12 infection was 169 and 254, respectively.
source: Quantification of ChIP-Seq input reads allowed us to determine that the approximate number of genomes per cell in WT and n12 infection was 169 and 254, respectively (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is calculated from ChIP-Seq input data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The genome number per cell is consistent with infecting at an MOI of 10 pfu/cell and an approximately particle to pfu ratio of 20–30.
source: This value is consistent with infecting at an MOI of 10 pfu/cell and an approximately particle to pfu ratio of 20–30.
evidence: This is inferred from the calculated genome number and known infection parameters.
